alt: A source emits radiation in all directions and a Geiger-Müller tube intercepts only a small fraction, plus background radiation. Activity is decays per second in the source, measured in becquerels (1 Bq = 1 decay per second, 1 kBq = 1000 Bq, 1 MBq = 1 000 000 Bq). Count rate is what the detector records, in counts per second or per minute, and is normally much less. Both halve in one half-life.
caption: Activity is in Bq; a detector gives a count rate in counts per second or minute.

after: ## The time units: second, minute and hour
alt: 1 h = 60 min = 3600 s. Counts per second × 60 gives counts per minute, and counts per minute ÷ 60 gives counts per second; per minute is the bigger number. Put elapsed time and half-life in the same unit before dividing, and reading and background per the same time unit before subtracting.
caption: Use 60, not 100, and match the time units before dividing or subtracting.

alt: A Geiger-Müller tube is moved away from an alpha source in centimetre steps. A sketch graph of count rate against distance in cm stays high close to the source, then drops to the background level within a few centimetres, because alpha particles stop after a few cm of air.
caption: Alpha travels only a few centimetres in air, so the count falls to background.

alt: A source of half-life 45 min has activity 3200 Bq. 3.0 h = 180 min, which is 180 ÷ 45 = 4 half-lives. Bars to scale show 3200, 1600, 800, 400 and 200 Bq at 0, 45, 90, 135 and 180 min, so the activity is 200 Bq.
caption: Convert 3.0 h to 180 min first: four half-lives take 3200 Bq to 200 Bq.

alt: A G-M tube records 1260 counts in 3.0 minutes, a measured rate of 420 counts/min. The background of 0.40 counts per second is 24 counts/min. The corrected count rate is 420 − 24 = 396 counts/min, which is 6.6 counts/s.
caption: Put the background in the same time unit as the reading before subtracting.

alt: Activity falls 6000 → 3000 → 1500 → 750 Bq, three half-lives in 15 h, so the half-life is 15 ÷ 3 = 5.0 h. This equals 5.0 × 60 = 300 min, and 300 × 60 = 18 000 s.
caption: Count the halvings, divide the time, then convert: 5.0 h = 300 min = 18 000 s.
